citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley, UChicago)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) sourced from high school math competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, a final boxed answer, a difficulty level from 1 to 5, and spans seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
name: MATH
rai:annotatorDemographics: For human evaluation, six university students studying computer science participated. Four participants are authors on the paper. The other two are friends or acquaintances of the authors. All participants gave consent. Participants had one hour to complete 20 problems without a calculator. The paper notes that crowdsourcing (e.g., Amazon Mechanical Turk) was not feasible due to the strong mathematical background required.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human evaluation was conducted on a random sample of 20 problems from the MATH test set. Results: one participant (does not like math) scored 40%; one ambivalent participant scored 65%; two participants who like math scored 70% and 75%; one participant with AMC 10 perfect score and USAMO attendance scored 90%; one three-time IMO gold medalist scored 90% (missed questions exclusively due to small arithmetic errors).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems are tagged by difficulty from 1 to 5 following AoPS conventions. A subject's easiest problems are assigned difficulty level 1 and hardest problems level 5. For example, the first few problems of an AMC 8 exam are often level 1, while AIME problems are level 5. Each problem also has a subject tag from seven categories: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more. Many problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems are formatted in LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language, with step-by-step solutions and final boxed answers.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging even for humans: a computer science PhD student attained approximately 40% accuracy, and a three-time IMO gold medalist attained 90%. Large language models achieved only 3.0% to 6.9% accuracy. The authors note that simply increasing model size will be impractical for achieving strong mathematical reasoning if scaling trends continue, suggesting the dataset may require new algorithmic advancements to solve.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions encoded with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients encoded without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent representations (e.g., \frac{x}{y} and \dfrac{x}{y}, \left( and (, 0.5 and 1/2) are treated as equivalent. Units may be included or omitted; spaces are ignored.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model would be impressive but have ramifications for cheating on homework. They explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. Solving the MATH dataset with machine learning would be of profound practical and intellectual significance given the broad reach and applicability of mathematics.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; measuring reasoning capabilities; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; forecasting reasoning capabilities of AI systems. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: None. The dataset consists of mathematics competition problems and solutions with no personal or sensitive information.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not describe multiple independent annotations per item; difficulty and subject labels follow AoPS conventions rather than independent annotator judgments.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No annotation platform is described; difficulty labels follow AoPS conventions and the paper explicitly notes crowdsourcing was not feasible.
null_reasons.rai:dataBiases: The paper does not explicitly acknowledge biases in the MATH dataset or describe design decisions to avoid specific biases.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data handling for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is mentioned, though the paper notes competitions span decades.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection manipulation (augmentation, balancing, resampling) is described for the MATH dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools are described for the MATH dataset; difficulty labels follow AoPS conventions.
